title: Given a grid where each cell is empty, a fresh orange, or a rotten orange, every minute any fresh orange adjacent to a rotten one becomes rotten. Return the minimum minutes until no fresh orange remains, or negative one if impossible.

s1_definition.oneliner: Seed a BFS queue with all initially rotten cells at time zero, process level by level counting minutes, and return the elapsed time or negative one if any fresh cell remains unreachable.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Multi-source BFS** – all initially rotten cells are enqueued at time zero and advance in lockstep, so each BFS level represents one minute of rot spreading.
- **Fresh counter** – count fresh oranges up front and decrement each time one is rotted; if the counter reaches zero all oranges are rotten, otherwise some are unreachable.
- **Level-by-level processing** – process queue.size() cells per level, then increment the minute counter, ensuring each level adds exactly one minute.
- **Impossible case** – if fresh cells remain after the queue empties, return negative one.
- **Time complexity** – O(rows times cols) because each cell is enqueued at most once.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a fraud contagion starts with some flagged accounts. Each minute the flag spreads to directly linked clean accounts. Rajesh seeds the BFS with all initially flagged accounts at once and counts how many minutes until every reachable account is flagged. If some account cannot be reached from any flagged source, the contagion can never finish.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Rotting Oranges is a multi-source BFS problem where all initially rotten cells are seeded in the queue at time zero and spread rot in lockstep. Each BFS level represents one minute, and the number of levels is the minimum time to rot every reachable fresh orange. If any fresh orange remains unreachable after the queue empties, the answer is negative one.

The fresh counter is the clean way to detect the impossible case. Instead of rescanning the entire grid after BFS, count fresh oranges up front and decrement each time one is rotted. When the counter reaches zero, all fresh oranges were rotted. When the queue empties with the counter still positive, some orange was unreachable.

The key insight interviewers want is why multi-source BFS is correct: because all sources advance together in lockstep, the level count directly gives the time for the last orange to rot. Running separate BFS from each rotten cell would not measure the combined spread time correctly. This is equivalent to imagining a virtual super-source connected to all initially rotten cells.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this model for fraud contagion. Some accounts were flagged as compromised, and each minute the flag spread to directly linked clean accounts. Multi-source BFS computed the minimum time to flag every reachable account, and the fresh counter identified accounts that no compromised source could ever reach, which needed manual investigation.

Remember one sentence: seed multi-source BFS with all rotten cells at time zero, count levels for minutes, and use a fresh counter to detect unreachable oranges.

---

keyPoints: Seed the BFS queue with all initially rotten cells at time zero so they spread rot in lockstep.
Process the queue level by level where each level represents one minute of rot spreading.
Count fresh oranges up front and decrement on each rot; return negative one if any remain after BFS.
Multi-source BFS is equivalent to a virtual super-source connected to all initially rotten cells.
Time is O(rows times cols) because each cell is enqueued at most once.
Check fresh > 0 in the while condition to avoid overcounting minutes after all oranges are rotten.
